subject: Post-call: latency & throughput bands — Hosted vs Dedicated recommendation
messages:
From: Chloe Martin <chloe_martin@redwood.com>
To: Sam Chen <sam@fastretail.com>
Cc: Ben Carter <ben_carter@redwood.com>, Laura Bennett <laura_bennett@redwood.com>
Date: 2027-05-29T10:14:00-07:00
Subject: Post-call: latency & throughput bands — Hosted vs Dedicated recommendation

Hi Sam — thanks for the time earlier. Quick recap and a recommended next step so we can scope a pilot.

Call highlights (what I heard):
- Steady-state traffic: ~120 requests/sec (avg) for inference (text generation endpoint).
- Peak bursts: up to ~400 req/sec during sale windows (10–15 minute spikes).
- P95 latency target: <= 150 ms for single-turn responses (cost-sensitive on tail).
- Model footprint: currently evaluating a 30B-class open model; hope to use quantized variant.
- Data residency: US for now; may need EU in future.

Initial recommendation and tradeoffs:
- Hosted API: fastest onboarding, no infra to manage. Good if you want to start immediately and tolerate some performance variability — we can route to higher-capacity instances during spikes but SLA/throughput guarantees are lower.
- Dedicated (reserved capacity): recommended if you need predictable p95 latency and isolated capacity for consistent throughput. Better cost-per-token at scale and deterministic concurrency.
- Private/VPC: likely overkill for this stage unless procurement requires VPC/on-prem controls.

As next steps I need two quick confirms to propose a pilot:
1) Can you confirm the 120 req/sec steady and 400 req/sec peak numbers (are peaks sustained or short bursts)?
2) One-week pilot preference: do you want a Dedicated reserved pool with automatic fallback to Hosted during bursts, or start fully Hosted and migrate to Dedicated once QPS stabilizes?

Attached: a short SLA/ops deck and a benchmark matrix that maps sample QPS/latency bands to expected instance types and cost anchors.

If you want, Ben can pull together a 1-week pilot SOW and cost estimate. I copied Laura from our Solutions team for any architecture questions.

Thanks,
Chloe
Chloe Martin
Senior Account Executive, Redwood Inference
chloe_martin@redwood.com

Subject: Re: Post-call: latency & throughput bands — Hosted vs Dedicated recommendation

Thanks Chloe — good summary. A couple clarifications:
- The steady 120 req/sec is our average across daytime hours; peaks are short bursts (typically 5–12 minutes) but happen a few times per day during campaigns.
- Model will be generator for simple product descriptions (~200 tokens avg). We expect to test a 30B quantized model as you noted.
- Cost is a big factor for us — procurement is looped (procurement@fastretail.com) and will need cost anchors for both Hosted and Dedicated.
- We’ll need SOC2 type II evidence and an idea of audit logs retention before procurement can move fast.

Prefer to start with a Dedicated pilot if cost looks reasonable — deterministic latency is a higher priority than zero-ops for the first trial.

Sam Chen

Sam — appreciate the clarity. Quick cost/ops anchors to help procurement:
- Hosted: estimated $0.045–0.06 per generated token for the 30B quantized path at your QPS profile (higher variability during bursts). Pros: no infra commit; cons: less predictable tail latency and no capacity isolation.
- Dedicated (reserved pool): ballpark $8k–$12k/month per reserved GPU pool node depending on instance type and commitment. For your 120 avg / 400 burst profile we’d likely recommend a 3-node reserved pool with autoscale headroom for bursts (combined with prefix caching). That produces a predictable p95 in the 80–140 ms range in our tests.

Proposal for pilot (if you’re comfortable):
1) 1-week Dedicated reserved pilot sized to match the 120 avg and absorb 400 burst using short autoscale headroom.
2) Canary fallback to Hosted for any unexpected overrun.
3) Deliverables: performance report, cost breakdown, and an ops runbook.

I’ll draft a one-week SOW and cost anchor — attached a generic SOW template; Chloe, can we get procurement’s preferred billing terms?

Ben Carter
Solutions Engineer, Redwood Inference
